If you are installing Miniconda on Windows and are getting an error like the one in the screenshot below, read on.

That error usually isn’t a Python problem — the installer extracted the packages fine but got blocked when it tried to write them into C:\Users\█████\miniconda3. This is most likely due to an access violation of some kind.

If this happens, hit Abort rather than Ignore. An ignored link failure gives you a broken environment that fails in confusing ways later :-(

In any case, follow these steps to fix the problem:

Delete the failed install folder. d

Remove C:\Users\█████\miniconda3 entirely before retrying. A partially-linked directory from the aborted attempt will make the next install fail the same way.

Also check for a stale .conda folder in your user directory and delete that too.

Turn off real-time protection temporarily.

In Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings, switch off Real-time protection. Conda creates thousands of hardlinks very fast, which AV heuristics frequently flag.

Also check Ransomware protection > Controlled folder access and disable it.

Turn both back on after the install finishes.

Steps 1 and 2 together resolve the large majority of these problems. If not, follow these steps:

Check whether your user folder is in OneDrive.

If the Documents folder is synced to OneDrive, the sync client can lock files mid-install.

Pause OneDrive syncing, or better: install somewhere outside the user profile entirely, like C:\miniconda3.

Re-run the installer as administrator.

Right-click the .exe file and choose Run as administrator.

Pick ‘Just Me’ when asked about install scope.

Install to a short path with no spaces or non-ASCII characters to avoid a separate class of linking failures.

Re-download if it still fails.

In this Lab, you will set up your coding environment so that you can do all the work required in this class. These instructions provide a high-level description of what you need to do; for each task, there are help docs that you can branch out to if you are unsure of what to do.

Tip

You are encouraged to collaborate with your colleagues to get these things done.

For your files:

It is essential for this class and all other data science courses that you have a place to put your code and a way to share it with others.

A private GitHub repository for your coursework. In general, when you submit homework, you will submit a URL to a notebook in your repo. To use GitHub, you will need to install a couple of other things, such as Git and SSH.

A local directory (aka folder) on your computer’s file system in which you will clone this repo using Git, and where you will conduct all the work for this class.

For your code:

Here is a list of all the software requirements for this class. This is often called your “stack.”

A working installation of Python, a popular programming language for data science. We will be using version 3.12, which is not the latest one. You will define this in your environment (see next item).

A dedicated Python environment for this class with the right versions of Python and required modules. We recommend using conda for this, a command line tool that comes with Miniconda (see below).

A collection of Python libraries that you will use throughout the course, including Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, SciPy, and Plotly. Other libraries will be specified as needed.

VS Code or Jupyter Lab, two programming editors. If you use VS Code, you will need to install the extensions for Python and Jupyter.

Jupyter notebooks will be the primary file format for this course. Although not a separate piece of software per se, it is worth highlighting this since these notebooks, which end in .ipynb are not standard Python files, which end in .py.

Note

Although this seems like a lot of stuff, each task just requires following the steps, i.e. there’s no problem solving -- just patience and attention to detail! If you are uncomfortable with the command line, then this will help you become acquainted with it. Also: you will use each of these things throughout your career as a student of data science at UVA.

On a Mac, it’s here:/Users/[Username]/Documents

Of course, you need to replace [Username] with the user name you use to log onto your computer.

In this directory you will put any files that are important for this class. You will also clone your course repo here.

A Python environment is a separate installation of Python on your system that will contain a specific version of Python and custom collection of libraries. Environments allow you to make sure you have the right combinations and versions of libraries so that they don’t conflict with each other.

Note

In this course, we will be using specific versions of libraries, like Pandas, because they have features that previous versions do not.

In this course we use Jupyter Notebooks.

Jupyter -- which is a portmantaeu of Julia, Python, and R -- refers to a platform that let’s you run Python code interactively and literately.

Interactively: Code is run in cells and the output of the code is printed below the cell. If the output is graphical, this is output too.

Literately: You can write either blocks of code or Markdown to alternate between code and text. This allows you to compose your script as a narrative, something that can be understood by others -- as well as your later self :-)

In this notebook, we highlight some feature of Jupyter Notebooks to keep in mind when using them.

A Jupyter notebooks is actually a JavaScript file that is run in a browser.

JavaScript is the native programming language of web browswers.

The browser executes the script, which produces an interactive application.

Jupyter notebook files end in .ipynb.

Jupyter notebook files are typically created within a programming editors, such as VS Code or Jupyter Lab

Caution

Jupyter files are not Python scripts. Python scripts, which typically end in .py, are plain text files that must be run from the command line with the python interpreter.

Every notebook, in order to run the code they contain, is associated with a kernel.

A kernel is just an instance of an interpret, such as Python or R. Is it associated with an environment that contains various libraries and versions.

The way you select a kernel depends on the editor your are using.

Kernels can be changed.

Kernels often need to be restarted.

When shutting down a notebook, kernels need to be shut down, too.

The markdown cells in a notebook are as important as the code cells.

They provide context and explanation for the code.

Jupyter notebooks can in fact be used to write scientific (and other) articles.

Markdown is an abbreviated syntax for generating HTML.

To use it effectively, you should understand how HTML structures documents.

These are the main elements of HTML that Markdown lets yu

Headers define sections and subsection of a document.

Paragraphs define chunks of text.

Lists define numbered or unnumbered lists of items.

Links define hypertext links to other documents.

Images define embedded images.

And so on.

Here is 

GitHub’s documentation on the flavor of Markdown they use.

A very cool thing about markdown is that it allows you to embed other formatting languages. For example, you can write \LaTeX:$x^2 + y_1 = z$

produces

x^2 + y_1 = z

And$$

$$

```

Since Jupyter notebooks let you run code in any order — i.e. out of order, from a programming perspective — you can get into trouble.

Re-running a cell may break if it changes the value of variable on which it depends.

The solution is to re-run your notebook often.

But be careful here, too: You may have deleted a cell that defines something that another cell depends on. When you restart the kernel an rerun the cells, the cell with the dependency will fail and throw an error.

Note

Information organized as a set of atomic facts is more typical than you might expect. Any time a survey is a taken, researchers collect such facts and then compile them into tables for analysis. Even scientific experiments can be like this: think of how data are collected into log books and then organized into tables.

Let’s go through this process again, with a slightly more complex example.

Consider the following descriptive statement, a sentence you might find in a report on global health.

“In 1970, Germany spent $USD 252.311 per capita and had a life expectany of 70.6 years.”

Now, this sentence can be decomposed into a set of atomic facts.

We might write down these facts like this:Observation1 country Germany
Observation1 year 1970
Observation1 spending 252.311
Observation1 life_expectancy 70.6

Note that in writing these doown we have surfaced something interesting -- the implicit subject of the sentence is the observation.

This is a little tricky, because it looks like the the subject is the country. But the year 1970 is not a property of Germany!

Now, imagine we have a bunch of these sets of facts, one set for each country in the world and year between 1970 and 2020.

A segment of these data might look like the following multi-line Python string:

data = """
Observation1 country Germany
Observation1 year 1970
Observation1 spending 252.311
Observation1 life_expectancy 70.6
Observation2 country France 	
Observation2 year 1970 	
Observation2 spending 192.143 	
Observation2 life_expectancy 72.2

Observation4 spending 150.437
Observation4 life_expectancy 72.0
Observation5 country USA
Observation5 year 1970
Observation5 spending 326.961
Observation5 life_expectancy 70.9 
"""

Let’s use Pandas to convert these facts into a table

We’ll use a list comprehension to parse the string into a list of lists and pass that to a data frame constructor.

lol = [row.split() for row in data[1:-1].split("\n")]
lol



import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(lol, columns=['Subject','Predicate','Object'])
df

Now, the shape of this table is not how we normally want our data.

It shows how the data set is composed of facts, but it’s not useful in this form for data analysis.

For one thing, the Object column contains data of different types, which prevents storing them and processing them properly.

One thing we can do is pivot the table into this form:

df1 = df.pivot(index='Subject', columns='Predicate', values='Object')
df1



We see that that the pivot operation sorted the columns alphatically.

A more intuitive way of represented the data is as follows:

df1[['country','year','spending','life_expectancy']]



In this version of the table, the columns show the common pattern of the descriptive sentence: “Country A in year B spent C dollars per capita and had a life expectancy of D.” The sentence encodes a hypothesized cause and effect relationship: what factors influence life expectancy?

Important

This puts our data into “tidy” form -- each row is a unique observation, and each column is unique feature, or variable.

We have seen that a table can be constructed from a collection of atomic facts.

Each atomic fact has a three-part structure: Subject, Predicate, Object.

The subject of an atomic fact is often observation itself.

These parts can be mapped onto a table as rows, columns, and cells.

Tables are a primary form of visualizing linguistic information.

Important

The lesson here is that to understand a table, you first need to understand that implied structure of the atomic facts it represents. To identify the proper subject of these facts is to understand what the data are about.

Generate a collection of atomic facts by describing something and collecting the data in a spreadsheet.

Then convert the data in the spreadsheet to a table where rows are subjects and columns are predicates.

We have seen that a tidy table is one in which:

Each row stands for a unique observation. The observation is the subject of the recorded fact.

Each column stands for a variable. The variable is the predicate of the recorded fact.

Each cell possesses the value of that variable for a given observation. The value is the object (so-called) of the recorded fact.

In this notebook, we will look at how to use grouping variables to aggregate measurement data and to generate wide tables.

We will work with the mpg dataset from Seaborn.

Note

The data represent fuel efficiency and engine attributes for 398 automobile models from 1970 to 1982. It is originally from the StatLib library and the 1983 ASA Data Exposition.

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

mpg = sns.load_dataset('mpg')
mpg

Get the column names and classify them into lists.

mpg.columns

group_cols = ['origin', 'model_year'] # Does not form a key
measure_cols = ['mpg', 'cylinders', 'displacement', 'horsepower', 'weight', 'acceleration']



Re-order the dataframe.

mpg[id_cols + group_cols + measure_cols]



Note

If we wanted to, we could extract a variable for car manufacturer like so:mpg['make'] = mpg['name'].str.split().str[0]

This would give us another grouping variable to work with.

Grouping columns and measurement columns have a complementary relationship to each other.

Let’s look at how we can use group variables to do aggregation on the measurement variables.

To do this, we use Pandas’ groupby function. This function takes a list of columns to group on, followed by a list of columns to which an aggregating function can be applied. If no columns are specified for the aggregation, then all columns are used.

Here we group our table by the variable origin and get the mean value of each measurment variable.

mpg.groupby('origin')[measure_cols].mean()



And here we group by model_year and get the means.

mpg.groupby('model_year')[measure_cols].mean()

We can also group by and aggregate on two variables.

mpg.groupby(group_cols)[measure_cols].mean()

The pattern we are using here is called “split-apply-combine” strategy for data analysis, a term coined by 

Hadley Wickham (2011). Recall that he also coined the expression “tidy data”.

It refers to the process of ...

SPLITTING a table in separate tables based on the domain of a group variable,

APPLYING an aggregate function, like mean or sum, to each group independenty,

and then taking the resulting rows and COMBINING them into a new table.

The resulting table has a row for each unique group value — i.e. the resulting table contains the domain of the grouping column.




source

Note the structure of the tables that result from aggregating with groupby: The all have indexes that consist of the domains of the group variables, or every combination of them if grouping on more than one variable.

Tip

Indexes are an important concept in Pandas. They look like regular columns, but they behave a little differently. We’ll learn more about this behavior as we apply Pandas to different datasets and problems.

One of the interesting things you can do with a dataframe that has at least two index columns and one measurement column is unstack it.

Let’s regenerate the aggregate table on our two group variables and save it to a new dataframe.

mpg_agg2 = mpg.groupby(group_cols)[measure_cols].mean()
mpg_agg2.head()



Now let’s use the unstack method to project the domains of the two group variables onto the two axes.

We also use the transform function T to turn the table sideways, which gives us countries as columns.

mpg_agg2['mpg'].unstack().T



mpg_agg2['mpg'].unstack().T.plot(title="MPG");



mpg_agg2['horsepower'].unstack().T



mpg_agg2['horsepower'].unstack().T.plot(title="Horsepwer");

We can use pivot_table to do an aggregated pivot.

This function is like pivot from the previous notebook, but requires an aggregate function.

mpg.pivot_table(index='model_year', columns='origin', values='mpg', aggfunc='mean')

Why can’t we just use pivot?

We noted above that the group cols do not form a unique key.

Let’s demonstrate what this means by attempting to pivot the dataset on the group variables a measurement.

try:
    mpg.pivot(index='model_year', columns='origin', values='mpg')
except ValueError as e:

Caution

There is a difference between the pivot function and the pivot_table function. The former assumes that the index, columns, and values are direct transformations of observations, whereas the latter applies an aggregate function to groups of observations.

The question to ask in choosing between the two is: Does the combination of group variables — being used to define the index and columns in the pivot — produce a unique set of combination or not? If they do form a key, then use pivot, if they do not, use pivot_table. In any case, if you use pivot incorrectly, you will get an error.

mpg.value_counts(group_cols).unstack().T



We can clearly see that the data are imbalanced relative to origin.

This notebook covers some of the basics of using Pandas.

It is meant to get you acquainted with how Pandas does some common data operations, not to provide in depth coverage of the library.

Basic operations include filtering and selecting data from an existing dataset.

In this notebook, We will use the nycflights13 dataset, which contains every flight that departed from a New York City airport in 2013. The data comes from the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

Here is a data dictionary for the dataset:

Variable Name

Data Type

Description

year, month, day

Integer

Date of departure.

dep_time, arr_time

Integer

Actual departure and arrival times (Format: Local time, HHMM or HMM). Missing values (NA) represent canceled flights.

sched_dep_time, sched_arr_time

Integer

Scheduled departure and arrival times (Format: Local time, HHMM or HMM).

dep_delay, arr_delay

Float

Departure and arrival delays, measured in minutes. Negative times represent early departures/arrivals.

carrier

String

Two-letter airline carrier abbreviation (maps to the airlines table).

flight

Integer

Flight number.

tailnum

String

Aircraft tail number (maps to the planes table). Missing values (NA) represent canceled flights.

origin

String

Origin airport code (EWR, JFK, or LGA; maps to airports and weather).

dest

String

Destination airport code (maps to airports).

air_time

Float

Amount of time spent in the air, measured in minutes.

distance

Float

Distance between origin and destination airports, measured in miles.

hour, minute

Float

Scheduled departure time broken down into hour and minute components.

time_hour

datetime

Scheduled date and time of the flight formatted as a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS). Used for joining directly with the weather table.

If you are currently writing code, let me know if you need help with a specific programming language (like R or Python) or a particular data manipulation query (such as calculating average delays by carrier).

import pandas as pd

flight_data_url = "https://virginia.box.com/shared/static/hby5hxuvurkmatdxgy0p1ua7oftwl6i9.csv"
flights = pd.read_csv(flight_data_url)

This dataset contains all 336,776 flights that departed New York City in 2013.

flights

The .info() method gives a compact structural overview: column names, data types, and how many non-missing values each column has.

This gives us information on the name and data type of each column, as well as how many non-null values are in each column.

flights.info()



Note

Pandas data types (Dtype) like int64, float64, object (usually strings), and datetime64 matter for the same reason data types always do: the operations you can perform on a column depend on its type.

hierarchy.lvl3: A quick note on Pandas’ methods
A quick note on Pandas’ methods

records.content:
Most of Pandas’ core operations are methods.

Tip

Remember that in object-oreinted parlance a method is a function attached to an object. The object in most cases is the dataframe. In some cases, though, Pandas’ methods are attached to the Pandas object itself, i.e. pd.

These are called with . directly on the object, in this case flights.

For example, to get the top rows in a dataframe, we call the .head() method.

flights.head()

hierarchy.lvl2: How many rows and columns are in the dataframe?
How many rows and columns are in the dataframe?

records.content:
The number of rows and columns in a dataframe is called its shape.

You access this information by calling the dataframe’s shape attribute, like so:

flights.shape



Note that it returns a tuple.

If you were only interested in findout out how many rows are in the dataset, you can do this:

flights.shape[0]



Or, you could use Python’s len() function, which works on any list-like object:

len(flights)



Caution

The shape returned by .shape will show the number of columns in the dataframe excluding any index columns.

Always begin by asking this question.

If they data are not tidy, what shape are they in (literally)?

Does the dataset need to be reshaped in any way?

If they are tidy, what is the unit of observation?

In this case, the dataset is tidy and the unit of obseration is the specific flight -- the taking off and landing of a specific airplane.

The next thing to do is identify the column types.

Are there any identifiers? Groupers? Measurements?

Are there any redundant columns? These are columns that repeat data in other columns.

Are there any analytical columns? These are columns that are computed from one or more other columns.

Here, we grab the list of columns from the dataset using the columns attribute of the dataframe.

Using the information we got from .info(), we can identify the column uses.

Note we are using the column number offsets to combine slices of the column list to create our new lists.

cols = list(flights.columns)
cols



group_cols = cols[1:4] + cols[10:15] + cols[17:19]
group_cols



measure_cols = cols[4:10] + cols[15:17]
measure_cols



There are no identifying columns, and there are two redundant ones: time_hour and Unnamed: 0.

The Unnamed: 0 column is an artifact of the import process. It gave this name to the unnamed first column in the CSV file, which clearly stands for the row number.

Tip

To avoid this kind of spurious column naming, you can tell Pandas to treat the first column as an index by setting the argument index_col to 0 in the read_csv function:flights = pd.read_csv(flight_data_url, index_col=0)

To see how this works, try replacing the line of code above where we import the dataset with this one.

One of the most important operations to perform on a dataframe is filtering.

Filtering grabs a subset of rows based on some specified conditions.

Important

Filtering is a row-wise operation: We use it to extract a subset of rows that meet certain conditions.

For example, we may want to see only rows for a certain year and month.

We can use .query() to do this. It works by passing a condition expressed as a string.

For example, to see all flights for February 2013, we would do this:

flights.query("year == 2013 & month == 2")



Here is a query for flights delayed more than 120 minutes:

flights.query("dep_delay > 120")

You also filter by supplying the two expressions directly to the dataframe’s indexer, which you can access by using two square brackets at the end of the variable name, e.g. flights[].

Note that the two boolean expressions are enclosed in parentheses.

flights[(flights['year'] == 2013) & (flights['month'] == 2)]

You can also query by using Pandas’ loc accessor method to do queries.

flights.loc[flights['dep_time'] > 120]

The method .sort_values() changes the order of rows based on the value of one or more columns.

It takes a list of column names, or a single column name, to sort by.

The ascending argument determines the resulting sort order, whether from least to greatest (asending = True) or not. The default value is True, so if we want reverse sort order we set it to False.

flights.sort_values('dep_delay', ascending=False)



Note that the number of rows hasn’t changed. Sorting rearranges the data, it doesn’t filter it.

.drop_duplicates() finds unique rows in a dataset.

flights1 = flights.drop_duplicates()



We can compare the lenghts of the two dataframes to see if there are any duplicates.

len(flights) == len(flights1)



Turns out there aren’t.

You can create new columns by naming them in the indexer and then assigning a value to them.

Let’s compute the gain (how much time a delayed flight made up in the air) and the speed in miles per hour:

flights['gain'] = flights['dep_delay'] - flights['arr_delay']
flights['speed'] = flights["distance"] / flights["air_time"] * 60
flights



Note

These new columns are what we have been called “analytical” columns. They are direct transforamtions of the data and don’t add any new empirical information to the dataset.

Another important operation to perform on a dataframe is to select a subset of columns.

Sometimes you do this because there are too many columns to see on one page. Other times, you want to zoom in on a few columns for exploratory purposes.

Important

Selecting is a column-wise operation. We use it to select a subset of columns from the dataframe.

To select columns, we just pass a list of column names to the dataframe.

flights[["year", "month", "day"]]



Note that we can pass a list of columns in a different order than how they appear in the dataframe.

flights[["year", "day", "month"]]



We can also select a range of columns by position with loc method.

The : in the expression below means all rows — we’ll look at this function more below.

flights.loc[:, "year":"day"]



We can use our column lists from above to select, too.

flights[group_cols]



flights[measure_cols]

hierarchy.lvl2: Combining filtering and selecting with loc
Combining filtering and selecting with loc

records.content:
With the loc method, you can combine filtering and selecting.

In the first argument, you can put a filtering expression. This is usually a boolean expression applied to one or more columns in the dataframe.

In the second argument, you can put a selecting expression. The is usually a list of columns names.

Think of it this way:df.loc[rowwise_expression, columnwise_expresson]

For example:

flights.loc[flights.month == 1, ['dep_time','dep_delay']]

The whole point of a dataframe is to be able to compute statistical and other mathematical properties from the data.

Here are a couple of quick things you can do.

hierarchy.lvl3: Get the number of values in a column or combination of columns with value_counts
Get the number of values in a column or combination of columns with value_counts

records.content:
You can use value_counts() to quickly count the number of rows associated with one or more columns:

flights.value_counts('carrier')



flights.value_counts(['origin','dest'])



Note that value_counts returns a series , not a dataframe.

If want a dataframe, we can use the .to_frame() method.

flights.value_counts(['origin','dest']).to_frame('n')



Note also the .value_counts() returns a series with an index for the counted columns.

When we have at least two grouping columns in the index, unstack the results, since the count is a measurement.

Here we see a wide table showing the top 20 most frequent origin and destination combinations.

flights.value_counts(['origin','dest']).head(20).unstack(fill_value=0)

You can compute aggregate values in many ways in Pandas. Here are two of the most common.

One is to just apply the aggregate function to one or more columns.

Here we get the mean value of each of our measurement columns.

flights[measure_cols].mean()



We can also pass the aggregation funcfion name to the .agg() method.

flights[measure_cols].agg('mean')



The .agg() method has the advantage of being able to take more than one function.

Here we get the mean, median, and standard deviation.

flights[measure_cols].agg(['mean','median','std'])



We can transpose the table with the .T operator to turn the columns into observations.

flights[measure_cols].agg(['mean','median','std']).T

We can also use the .groupby() method to compute joint aggregate values on combinations of columns.

Here we get the mean values for all of our measure columns for each carrier to each airport.

flights.groupby(['carrier','dest'])[measure_cols].mean()



Note that .groupby() also returns a series with an index.

In this case, we can unstack the results on any of our aggregate measures, like so:

flights.groupby(['carrier','dest'])['dep_delay'].mean().unstack(fill_value=0).style.format(precision=0)

You’ve now seen several individual operations.

It is possible to combine these operations.

For example, if you wanted to find the fastest flights to Charlottesville’s CHO airport: you need to combine filtering, creating a new column, selecting columns, and sorting.

All in one pipeline:

flights.query('dest == "CHO"')\
    .groupby(["year", "month", "day"])\
    .agg(arr_delay=("arr_delay", "mean"))\
    .reset_index()\
    .head(10)



Note the use of backslashes. These allow us to write a single Python expression over multiple lines.

Instead of using backslashes, we can just wrap everything in parentheses.

(
    flights
    .query('dest == "CHO"')
    .groupby(["year", "month", "day"])
    .agg(arr_delay=("arr_delay", "mean"))
    .reset_index()
    .head()
)



Finally, here is the same set of operations using the indexer syntax.

(
    flights[flights['dest'] == 'CHO']
    .groupby(["year", "month", "day"])['arr_delay']
    .mean()
    .to_frame('arr_delay')
    .reset_index()
    .head()
)



Tip

You will find that in Pandas, the principle of TMTOWTDI — There’s More Than One Way To Do It — applies.
![bar-chart.png](attachment:6f6ecc53-269e-480c-b88e-bcaf5d37fde7.png)

A simple bar chart uses rectangular bars to represent and compare a numerical measurement variable over the domain of a group.

Groups (e.g., product types, months, or cities) are usually represented on the x axis.

Measurements (e.g., sales numbers, temperatures, or percentages) are usually represented on the y axis.

The height of each bar is proportional to the value it represents.

The width of the bar has no relationship to the value the bar represents.

Compare a measurement variable over a grouping variable, for example revenue by region, headcount per department, medals won by country, average rent in five cities, or votes per candidate.

Rank items from largest to smallest, for example a company’s top ten customers by spend, most common causes of support tickets, bestselling book titles, or the leading sources of a country’s emissions.

Compare a measurement variable over two or more grouping variables, for example quarterly revenue split by product line, survey answers by response option, budget by spending category across several years, or population by age band in each country.

Show deviation above and below a baseline with diverging bars, for example actual vs. budgeted spend per team, temperature anomalies by year, net sentiment scores by topic, or percentage change in sales by store.

Compare values across a small number of discrete time periods, for example annual profit for the last five years, quarterly enrollment, or headcount at the end of each fiscal year. In this case, time periods act as grouping variables.

hierarchy.lvl2: Creating a bar chart from scratch
Creating a bar chart from scratch

records.content:
We start with a data frame that contains a grouping variable with unique values and an associated measurement.

This is the simplest form of data that can be visualized with a bar chart.

In this case, a bar chart will show us visually the differences in magnitude among the values A, B, an C for the nominal feature.
First, let’s acquire the data.

In this case, we’ll just make them up.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns



my_data = [
	['A', 15],
	['B', 34],
	['C', 22]
]
df1 = pd.DataFrame(my_data)
df1



Before we plot anything, let’s properly label the axes in the data frame.

We will call the features group and measure.

Tip

It is highly recommended that you label your data frames before you plot their since these labels will be used by the visualization tool.

df1.columns = ['group', 'measure']
df1



Because the group data are unique, we can create a rudimentary bar chart just by converting the measurement value into a string.

To do this, we can use the handy .iterrows() method, which iterates over each row, returning the row index and row values each time.

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['group'], row['measure'] * '|')



We can improve the display by using the block character █ instead of a pipe:

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['group'], row['measure'] * '█')



We can even add the number value to make it more legible.

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['group'], row['measure'] * '█' + " " + str(row['measure']))



And — voilà! — you have a bar chart.

Now, to produce this kind of chart we call Pandas’ .plot() method and pass it the argument kind = 'bar' along with passing features to the x and y axes of the plot.

df1.plot(kind='bar', x='group', y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart")
plt.show()



Important

Stop and inspect the resulting chart.

Note where each element of the data frame lands on the chart:

variable

name \rightarrow

domain \rightarrow

value \rightarrow

group

x axis label

x axis scale

position of bars on the x axis

meausre

y axis label

y axis scale

height of bars on the y axis - group name $\rightarrow$ x axis label
- group domain $\rightarrow$ x axis scale
- group values $\rightarrow$ positions of bars on x axis
- measure name $\rightarrow$ the legend
- measure domain $\rightarrow$ y axis scale
- measure values $\rightarrow$ height of bars on y axis 

Let’s clean the figure up a bit.

First, let’s remove the legend since it is not really needed in this example.

Second, let’s rotate the letters on the x axis for readability.

df1.plot(kind='bar', x='group', y='measure', 
         title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", 
         legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



To create a horizontal chart, we set kind to barh.

df1.plot(kind='barh', x='group', y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



Note that instead of using the argument kind, we can call bar and barh as chained methods to .plot(), like so:

df1.plot.bar(x='group', y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()

Note that if we do not set the value of x, Pandas will use the index as the x axis.

df1.plot.bar(y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



In fact, it is a good practice to assign the grouping variable to be the index in this case.

Since the values are unique, they can used as index values.

df2 = df1.set_index('group')
df2.plot.bar(y='measure', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



Note also that if we pass a series to the plot method, by selecting a feature, we don’t need to specify the y argument either.

df2['measure']



df2['measure'].plot.bar(title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



Tip

This is an important pattern to remember: selecting and shaping your data before visualization often makes the visualization code simpler.

In the preceding example we had a data set in which unique grouping values are paired with measurements.

In reality, we don’t often get data like this. More typically, the grouping values are repeated over observations.

Consider the Iris data set, which we will grab from the Seaborn library.

iris = sns.load_dataset('iris')
iris.sample(10)



Notice the repetition of the grouping variable species.

To plot this variable against any of the other measurements, we need to group the measurements by the grouping variable and compute an aggregate value, such as the median, sum, or mean of the feature for each group.

To do this, we can use .groupby() as follows.

(
    iris.groupby('species').sepal_length.mean()
    .plot.bar(rot=0, title="Mean Sepal Length by Species")
)
plt.show()



Another thing we can do is just get the number of instances of a particular value in the nominal column using .value_counts().

iris.species.value_counts().plot.bar(rot=0)
plt.show()



Here we can see that the data set is balanced over species — there are 50 observations per species.

What if we want to compare the magnitudes of more than one measurement across a grouping variable, in this case species?

Let’s experiment to find out.

First, we get the mean of all the measurements by grouping on species and not specifying any columns to aggregate.

Pandas will interpret this as saying you want all the columns aggregated.

Note

You should only do this if the columns are all numeric and come from the same domain.

iris_means = iris.groupby('species').mean()
iris_means



Now, when we call plot.bar(), Pandas creates a bar chart for each variable and then combines them.

By default, it combines them into groups.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0)
plt.show()



We can also combine them by stacking if we set stacked = True.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0, stacked=True)
plt.show()



Finally, we can use subplot = True to create a separate plot for each feature.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0, subplots=True)
plt.show()



Notice that this figure needs some work to improve its legibility.

Let’s change the size of the figure to give each plot more room.

To do this, we set figsize = (5,10), i.e. we set width to 5 and height to 10 and remove the legend since it is redundant.

We can also set plt.tight_layout(), which adds spacing between the plots.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0, subplots=True, figsize=(5,10), sharey=True, legend=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Finally, we can transpose the table to change the priority of categories.

The order of representation is as follows: Each observation row gets a bar, and each feature column gets a plot.

So, if we want each species to get its own plot with features as bars, we can use the .T operator to flip the table.

iris_means.T



The result is a different bar plot.

Now, the variable names become the categories on the x axis.

iris_means.T.plot.bar(rot=0, subplots=True, figsize=(5,10), legend=False)
plt.show()



Of course, we can recreate the plots we made above with the new transposed table.

This plot shows the relative magnitudes of each measurement over species.

iris_means.T.plot.bar(rot=0, stacked=True)
plt.show()



iris_means.T.plot.bar(rot=0, stacked=False)
plt.show()

A pie chart is a circular graph used to display the relative magnitudes of a numeric measurement variable associated with a grouping variable.

For example, a grouping variable might be the types of food eaten during a day and the associated measurement might be number of calories.

The entire circle represents sum total of value of a given measurement, e.g. the total number of calories consumed in a day.

Each slice represents the contribution to the total by one of the group’s categoroes.

The area of the wedge is proportional to the magnitude of the measurement value for the category.

Pie charts typically use color to distinguish the different slices.

Viewing grouping variables whose domains constitute some whole, for example food types and diets, expenses and budgets, or investment options and portfolios.

Representing aggregate values for the domain of a grouping variable, where each slice represents a unique value and an associated statistic, such as its count or mean.

Note

The categories in the grouping variable domain should be disjoint, exhaustive, and relatively few in number.

Disjoint means that an obseration can have only one category value.

Exhaustive means that an observation my have one category value.

The meaning of few in number varies, but the idea is that there should not be so many slices on the pie that they can’t be visually distinguished.

Let’s create some imaginary data based the already described example — someone’s nutrient consumption in the course of a day by food type and measured in grams.

The pie will represent the total number of grams of food consumed by some person in a given day.

Each slice will represent on of the main nutrient groups — protein, fat, and carbohydrates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns



diet = pd.Series({
    'protein': 65,
    'fat': 40,
    'carbs': 18
})



diet.plot.pie()
plt.show()



With this pie chart, we can see clearly the relative amounts consumed from each food type.

The person appears to be on a low-carb diet.

Let’s now look at a classic data set — the Titanic data set.

This data set shows the survival rate of passengers on the ill-fated vessel that sank in 1912.

It consists almost entirely of nominal data for 1316 passengers.

These data are ideal for pie charts because:

Many variables represent exhaustive and exclusive groups, e.g. class and sex.

The number of values per feature is small.

We can use pie charts to display each feature’s composition.

titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
titanic.sample(10)



For convenience, let’s create a new feature age_group based on age to show if the person is an adult or child.

The converts the numberic variable age into a binary group.

titanic['age_group'] = np.where(
    (titanic['age'] >= 18)
    | titanic['who'].isin(['man','woman']), 
    'adult', 'child')



In addition, we are only interested in a subset of categorial columns, those that meet the criteria specified above, so we select those.

my_cols = ['sex', 'age_group', 'class','survived']
titanic = titanic[my_cols]
titanic.sample(10)



Now let’s create a pie chart for each of these features.

To do this, we create a list of aggregate data frames, one associated with each feature.

This is necessary because the slices of a pie chart must represent distinct categories.

dfs = {}
for col in my_cols:
    dfs[col] = titanic.value_counts(col)



for col in dfs:
    df = dfs[col]
    df.plot.pie(title=col.title(), figsize=(2,2))
    plt.show()









A better way to show all for four pies is with a grid of subplots.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6,6))
for i, col in enumerate(titanic.columns):
    c = i % 2
    r = i // 2
    df = titanic.value_counts(col)
    df.plot.pie(title=col.title(), ax=ax[r,c])
plt.show()

We can see that there are two kinds of group variables in the Titanic data set:

those that define the social category of each person

one that defines the fate each person.

The first set may be thought of as input values and the second as the output.

Let’s group the data by social category and get the value counts of the survival variable.

This produces a data frame where the categorical features form the index and the survival feature is projected onto the column axis.

titanic_vc = titanic[my_cols].value_counts().unstack(fill_value=0)
titanic_vc.columns = ['no','yes']
titanic_vc



We can use the survival rate data to compute a rough probability estimate s_rate  as follows.

# titanic_vc['s_rate'] = titanic_vc.div(titanic_vc.sum(axis=1), axis=0).yes
titanic_vc['s_rate'] = titanic_vc['yes'] / titanic_vc[['no','yes']].sum(axis=1)
titanic_vc.sort_values('s_rate')



In this form, the table lets us ask questions like:

“If a passenger was a first class adult male, what was their chance of surviving?”

Since these data are exhaustive, exclusive, and relatively few, we can use a pie chart to visualize the probabilities.

Caution

Although the categories are exhaustive and exclusive in this example, the probabilities represented by the pie do not sum to 1.

This is because each value is a conditional probability given a combination of categorical features.

titanic_vc.s_rate.sort_values().plot.pie(title="Survual Rates")
plt.show()



How readable is this chart? Does it easily show which category combinations had the highest and lowest survival rates?

It turns out that pie charts become less useful as the number of categories increases.

In such cases, it is often better to fall back onto a bar chart.

The one below clearly shows which categories had the highest and lowest survival rates.

ax = titanic_vc.s_rate.sort_values().plot.barh()
plt.show()



Note

Be careful not to read too much into the survival rates of the first and second class children.

Their total numbers are much smaller than the other categories.

Below, we visualize the fate of the adult passengers.

(
    titanic_vc
        .query("age_group == 'adult'")
        .s_rate
        .sort_values()
        .plot
        .pie(title="Survival Rates of Adults")
)
plt.show()

Panda’s pie charts come with some useful arguments to improve their display.

These are:

autopct: to label slides with their associated percentages.

explode: to pull out a slide for emphasis.

starting: to orient the pie so that the first cut appears at the degree of your choice.

To use the autopct argument, you can pass a standard Python formatting string to autopct to control decimal places.

autopct='%1.1f%%': Displays one decimal place (e.g., 12.5\%).

autopct='%1.2f%%': Displays two decimal places (e.g., 12.50\%).

autopct='%1.0f%%': Rounds to the nearest whole integer (e.g., 13\%)

Note

THe autopct argument here is using Python’s % formatting style. To learn more about it, check out this 

article.

feature_name = 'survived'
dfs[feature_name].plot.pie(autopct='%1.2f%%', title=feature_name.title())
plt.show()



Here’s how you can pull out a slide to emphasize it.

explode_tuple = (0, 0.1, 0) 
dfs['class'].plot.pie(autopct='%1.2f%%', explode=explode_tuple)
plt.show()



Note that you can pull out more than one slice.

explode_tuple = (0.1, 0.1, 0.1) 
dfs['class'].plot.pie(autopct='%1.2f%%', explode=explode_tuple)
plt.show()



Finally, here’s how you can reorient the pie using startangle.

Here we set the value to 90\degree, which corresponses to the 12:00 position of a clock.

dfs['class'].plot.pie(autopct='%1.2f%%', startangle=90)
plt.show()

Bar charts show measurement variables associated with the domains of group variables.

Pie charts show measurement variables associated with the domains of group variables where the domain values are exhaustive, exclusive, and relatively few.

Line charts allow us to visualize measurement variables where the x axis consists of a group or measurement variable whose domain is sequential, e.g. a calendar date.

Show trends where x axis represents time, for example monthly revenue over a fiscal year, daily average temperature, a patient’s blood pressure across visits, website traffic per week, or population by decade.

Compare trends, for example sales of three product lines side by side, unemployment rates in several countries, control vs. treatment groups in a trial, or actual vs. forecast budget.

Plot classical mathematical functions, e.g. linear functions like y = mx + b, for example the parabola y = x^2, the sine wave y = \sin x, exponential decay y = e^{-kt}, or the hyperbola y = 1/x.

Show process types, for example the heating curve of water through its phase changes, a capacitor charging and discharging, or a stress–strain curve for a material under load.

Let’s look at a simple example.

Below, we visualize a small data set showing sales number over a series of years.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns



data = {
    'year': [2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026],
    'sales': [100, 120, 170, 160, 210, 240]
}
df1 = pd.DataFrame(data)
df1



To create a line graph in Pandas, you can just call .plot() by itself.

Line graphs are the default plot type.

In the example below, we set x to Year and y to Sales.

df1.plot(x='year', y='sales')
plt.show()



Of course, we can also call the .line() method explicitly.

df1.plot.line(x='year', y='sales')
plt.show()



Or we can set the kind argument to line

df1.plot(x='year', y='sales', kind='line')
plt.show()

In this example, we demonstrate how to plot more than one variable in the same figure.

We create data showing number of units sold per month for two products, A and B.

data = {
    'Month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May'],
    'Product_A': [15, 20, 35, 30, 45],
    'Product_B': [25, 18, 22, 40, 48]
}
df2 = pd.DataFrame(data)

df2.plot.line(x='Month', y=['Product_A', 'Product_B'], title="Business is Booming")
plt.show()



Note

It makes sense to show multiple lines in the same figure if their associated features have the same domain.

In the example both lines represent prices of products.

We can show the two lines on separate axes with the subplots argument set to True.

df2.plot.line(x='Month', y=['Product_A', 'Product_B'], subplots=True)
plt.show()

As we saw earlier, Pandas defaults to showing the index of a data frame on the x axis if x is left unspecified.

Here we set the index to Month, since the values are uniqure over the observations.

Then, since the remaining non-index features are related, we don’t need to specify those, either. Pandas assumes you want to show them all.

df3 = df2.set_index('Month')
df3.plot()
plt.show()



Here we change the style of plot to show points as well as lines.

df3.Product_A.plot.line(style = '-o')
plt.show()





We can set the attributes of multiple lines by passing lists to the arguments.

df3.plot.line(style=['o-', 's--'], color=['blue', 'green'])
plt.show()



Note that these data can be visualized with a bar chart.

However, they are better visualized with a line graph to show the trend of the data over the sequence.

The bar chart is useful here is you want to emphasize differences between A and B per month.

df3.plot.bar(rot=0)
plt.show()



Note

Line graphs and bar charts differ on how they represent domains on the x and y axis.

In contrast to a line graph, in a bar chart:

The years on the x axis are treated as categories.

The y axis is not clipped but begins with 0. As a rule, 

bar charts must have a zero baseline.

Let’s look at the mpg dataset provided by Seaborn.

Let’s use these data to see how cars in different coutries have changed over the years

mpg = sns.load_dataset('mpg')
mpg.head()



To compare measurements over year and origin, let’s create a wide table with hierarchical columns.

mpg_measures = ['horsepower','mpg','acceleration','weight']



mpg_wide = mpg.pivot_table(index='model_year', columns='origin', values=mpg_measures, aggfunc='mean')
mpg_wide



Note the structure of this table.

The series from the index will define the x-axis and the series associated with the columns will define separate y-axis values.

The result will be three plots for eacg aggregated feature.

Now, with the table structured this way, we can easily iterate through the measurement variables and generate graphs that compare origin values within each aggregated measure.

for measure_col in mpg_measures:
    mpg_wide[measure_col].plot(figsize=(6,3), title=measure_col)
plt.show()









Comparing these plots, we can see a couple of things.

First, as mpg went up during the 1970s, horsepower went down.

Second, the United States has favored horsepower over mpg in comparison to Europe and Japan.

What else can you see?

Let’s look another example the contains multiple measurements that can be plotted against time.

John Arbuthnot’s (1710) data set describes male and female births for London from 1629–1710.

Note

These time series data were used to carry out the first known significance test.

During every one of the 81 years, there were more male christenings (i.e. births) than female christenings.

As Arbuthnot asked, is this difference due to chance or did it mean the birth ratio was actually not 1:1?

# data_url = "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/HistData/Arbuthnot.csv"
data_url = "https://virginia.box.com/shared/static/tpree5hiavq5et794htm7208vc0anulm.csv"
dfx = pd.read_csv(data_url)
dfx.info()
dfx = dfx.set_index('Year')
dfx = dfx.drop("rownames", axis=1)
dfx.head()





Here are what the column names stand for:

Year:    The year, ranging from 1629 to 1710.

Males:   Number of male christenings (births).

Females: Number of female christenings (births).

Plague:  Number of deaths from the Plague.

Mortality: Total deaths (all causes combined) for that calendar year.

Ratio:   Ration of Males to Females.

Total:  The total number of births scaled in thousands (000s).

Now, let’s look at Total, the total number of births during this period.

dfx['Total'].plot(style='.-', legend=False, title="Total Births per Year")
plt.show()



For sake of comparison, look at how these same data appear when plotted as a bar chart. What differences do you notice in how the axes are represented?

dfx['Total'].plot.bar()
plt.show()



In any case, we can see a big trough between around 1640 and 1665.

Let’s look at all the variables together to see in any variables shed light on this.

To do this, we can use the subplots argument.

dfx.plot(subplots=True, figsize=(7.5,15))
plt.show()



It appears there are two general kinds of trend here — those that show births, and those that show deaths. It would be nice to compare them.

Let’s compare Total to Mortality.

dfx[['Total','Mortality']].plot()
plt.show()



This turns out to be not very useful.

The domains of the two variables are so different that one dwarfs the other.

One quick solution to this problem is to normalize both series by getting their Z-scores.zscore(x) = (x - \mu) / \sigma

dfx1 = dfx[['Total','Mortality']]
dfx1.columns = ['Births','Deaths']
(
    (dfx1 - dfx1.mean()) / dfx1.std()
).plot()
plt.grid()
plt.show()



But there is a better way, at least from the perspective of visualization.

hierarchy.lvl2: Showing two y-axis scales on the same axes
Showing two y-axis scales on the same axes

records.content:
When we compare two related variables come from different domains, it becomes a problem to show them on the same axes.

Matplotlib provides a function to solve this problem -- ax.twinx().

This function take the Axes object returned by a Pandas plot and creates a new Axes object that will be overlaid on the first.

In the result, the left spine represents the first plot while right spine represents the second.

ax = dfx1['Births'].plot(style='.-', legend=True)
ax2 = ax.twinx()
dfx1['Deaths'].plot(ax=ax2, color='orange', style='.-', legend=True)
ax.set_ylabel('Births'), ax2.set_ylabel('Deaths')
plt.title("Comparing Birth to Mortality")
plt.show()



Clearly, there is more work to make this plot production ready, but we are well on our way.

Line charts are also useful for plotting classicial mathematical functions, where y is a function of x, i.e. y = f(x).

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['x'] = np.arange(0, 5 * np.pi, 0.1)
df['sin_x'] = np.sin(df.x)
df.head()



df.plot(x='x', y='sin_x')
plt.grid()
plt.show()



df['cos_x'] = np.cos(df.x)
df.head()



df.plot(x='x', y=['sin_x','cos_x'])
plt.grid()
plt.show()

Area charts are essentially line graphs in which the area under the line is filled in with color.

By coloring in the area, the focus shifts from trends to the accumulation or composition of the value represented by the x axis.

There are two main types of area chart when they involve more than one trend line:

Overlapping: Area charts with multiple lines to make a comparison between groups.

Stacked: Area charts that show how a whole is divided into component parts.

Like bar charts and unlike line graphs, area charts should always have a zero baseline for the y axis.

In addtion, unlike bar charts, area charts tyoically do not show negative values.

Tracking time-series data, for example monthly sales revenue, daily stock prices, or annual website traffic.

Visualizing part-to-whole relationships over time, for example budget allocations by department or energy consumption by source.

Highlighting running totals, for example tracking total donations raised during a campaign or total active users acquired over a year.

Comparing lower and upper boundaries, such as minimum and maximum values, for example daily temperature highs and lows or financial confidence intervals.

In this example, we look at energy consumption by fuel type from 1870 to 2021.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

data_url = "https://virginia.box.com/shared/static/jdc6ao3aitrtjc2q4edfohupf0v3wyn5.csv"
energy = pd.read_csv(data_url).set_index('year')
energy.info()
energy





We alter the column names to simplify our visualization.

energy.columns = ['coal', 'gas', 'oil', 'other']



We also convert the index to a datatime data type.

Tip

Converting dates to datatime types improves how Pandas’ plot method interprets and displays the data.

energy.index = pd.to_datetime(energy.index.astype(str), format='%Y')
energy



Upon inspection, we notice a lot of null values.

We can interpret these as true absences, not faulty data collection.

energy = energy.fillna(0)
energy

In the chart below, the four lines and their areas are stacked on top of each other.

The chart shows both the overall growth of energy consumption and the relative contribution of each fuel.

You can see, for example, that before around 1945, coal is the dominant source of energy. After that, oil consumption grows to rival it.

plot_title = "Energy Consumption in the Long 20th Century"
energy.plot.area(title=plot_title)
plt.show()

If we set that stacked for False, what we see if the relative growth of each fuel type, but not the overall growth.

In this chart, we can see more clearly that although oil consumption grows rapidly after WWII, it still does not exceed the use of coal.

We can see, however, that from around the late 1960s to the turn of the century, gas use did exceed coal use.

energy.plot.area(stacked=False, title=plot_title)
plt.show()



Note that the unstacked chart is similar to the basic line graph in not showing combined amounts.

energy.plot(title=plot_title)
plt.show()

Now, if we want to show the relative amounts of fuel consumption over time without regard to absolute values, we can normalize the data so that the value of consumption for each year sums to 1.

This shows rather dramatically how the use of other fuels grow relative to coal.

energy_norm = energy.div(energy.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
# energy_norm = energy.apply(lambda x: x / x.sum(), axis=1) # Another way to compute this
# energy_norm = (energy.T / energy.T.sum()).T # Yet nother way to compute this
energy_norm



energy_norm.plot.area(title=plot_title + "\nRelative Consumption Rates")
plt.show()



Notice the margin at the top of this plot.

This is because Matplotlib pads the data range on each axis by 5%  so that lines and markers don’t sit flush against the spines.

To override this, you can grap the Axes object and change the value of the y axis limits.

ax = energy_norm.plot.area(title=plot_title + "\nRelative Consumption Rates")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
plt.show()



Or, you can just set the ylim argument in the plot method.

energy_norm.plot.area(title=plot_title + "\nRelative Consumption Rates", ylim=(0,1))
plt.show()

We can also show the normed data without stacking.

Again we see that coal consumption declines as oil increases.

We can also see clearly the period in which oil exceeds coal.

energy_norm.plot.area(stacked=False, title=plot_title)
plt.show()

Since we are showing composition of energy use, where the domain is small, we might compare area charts to pie charts.

Here is how we might accomplish the changing composition of energy use over time with pie charts.

First, let’s group our date by decade and get the means for each energy type.

# energy.index.year // 10 * 10



energy_decade = energy.groupby(energy.index.year // 10 * 10).mean().fillna(0)
energy_decade



# Plot the transpose to get a chart for each decade
ax = energy_decade.T.plot.pie(
    subplots=True, 
    figsize=(16,16), 
    legend=False, 
    layout=(4,4),  # Since there are 16 decades represented
    startangle=90,
)

# Loop through each axes object to clean things up
# Uncomment this block to see why we do this 
for i, ax in enumerate(ax.flatten()):
    ax.set_axis_off()
    my_label = energy_decade.index[i]
    ax.set_title(my_label)

plt.suptitle("Energy Consumption by Decade")
plt.show()

Let’s look more closely at the relationship between coal and oil after WWII.

A simple line graph shows the growth and competetion between the two.

coal_and_oil = energy.query("year >= 1945")[['coal','oil']]
plot_title2 = "Coal and Oil after WWII"
coal_and_oil.plot(title=plot_title2)
plt.show()



This is a good candidate for a difference chart, a variant of the area chart.

A difference chart is an area chart where only the areas of curve overlap are shaded.

A good example of this is William Playfair’s famous trade-balance chart from his Commercial and Political Atlas published in 1786:

Source: Wikimedia Commons

Heris a more contemporary example, showing the projected growth and decline of population segments in the United Sates:

Source: Eco3min

Let’s try to reproduce this effect with our energy dataset using Pandas and Matplotlib.

One approach is to create and plot a new column that consists of the minimum values of coal and oil.

To create it, we can get the row-wise .min() on the two variables.

coal_and_oil['min'] = coal_and_oil.min(axis=1)
coal_and_oil.head()



Then, If we plot min and set its color to white, it will mask everything except the overlaps.

Here’s how the three lines look as a line graph:

coal_and_oil.plot(title=plot_title2)
plt.show()



The min line overwrites the other two lines since it is drawn last.

Now let’s view them as an difference chart:

# First plot coal and oil
ax = coal_and_oil[['coal','oil']].plot.area(stacked=False)

# Then plot min as a mask
coal_and_oil['min'].plot.area(ax=ax, color='white', lw=0)

plt.show()



Note

You may be wondering why the min line does not have a legend associated with it.

This is because Pandas does not show a legend if the plot method is called on a series, as opposed to a dataframe.

Here we improve the way the bounding plot lines are colored.

# First plot coal and oil
ax = coal_and_oil[['coal','oil']].plot.area(stacked=False)

# Standardize the line colors
for line in ax.lines:
    line.set_color("black")

# Then plot min as a mask
coal_and_oil['min'].plot.area(ax = ax, color='white', lw=0)

plt.show()



# coal_and_oil['diff'] = abs(coal_and_oil['coal'] - coal_and_oil['oil'])
# coal_and_oil['diff'].plot()
# plt.show()



If you want to emulate the effect of the second example above, you can divide the data into two parts and plot the two with different styles.

We also add a point and line to emphasize the point of cross-over, although in this case the location is inexact.

Note that if you do this, you will need to specify the same colors for both plots. Otherwise, the Pandas and Matplotlib with pick new colors for the second plot.

Note

We we use the colors tab:blue and tab:orange here to preserve the original colors chosen by .plot().

These are names drawn from Tableau’s palette of colors.

We’ll cover color palettes in a later notebook.

# Define a cross-over year
cross_over_year = 2004

# First plot coal and oil before the date
ax = coal_and_oil.loc[coal_and_oil.index.year <= cross_over_year, ['coal','oil']]\
    .plot.area(stacked=False, ylim=(0, coal_and_oil.max().max()), color=['tab:blue','tab:orange'])

# The plot coal and oil after the date
coal_and_oil.loc[coal_and_oil.index.year >= cross_over_year, ['coal','oil']]\
    .plot.area(ax = ax, stacked=False, ls='--', color=['tab:blue','tab:orange'], legend=False)

# Add a point and to emphasize the cross-over
coal_and_oil.loc[coal_and_oil.index.year == cross_over_year, 'oil'].plot(style='o')
ax.axvline(f'{cross_over_year}-01-01', ls='--', lw=.5, c='gray')

# Standardize the line colors
for line in ax.lines:
    line.set_color("grey")

# Then plot min as a mask
coal_and_oil['min'].plot.area(ax = ax, color='white', lw=0)

plt.title("Coal Makes a Comeback")

plt.show()

Although each of these charts gives insight to energy consumption over time, it is important to convey to the reader just what they are looking at.

In particular, unless clearly labeled, it is easy to mistake a stacked area charted for an unstacked one.

In the plot below, the curves are stacked, but a reader might think that coal has the least usage since it is on the bottom.

Even if readers known that the plots are stacked, their eyes may deceive them into thinking that all of the fuel usages are always rising.

But we know that coal usage actually declines for something like a 40 year period.

energy.plot.area(stacked=True, title="Absolute Values")
plt.show()



Another source of confusion occurs when an area chart of normalized data is presented.

In the plot below, consider how the relative proportion of coal usage decreases even though the absolute usage increases.

energy_norm.plot.area(stacked=True, title="Relative Values", ylim=(0,1))
plt.show()

A scatter plot uses dots to represent the values of two numeric measurement variables on a cartesian plane.

The domains of the two variables are mapped onto the x and y axes to generate a 2D space.

Within this space, each dot on the plot represents an observation, i.e. a row of data.

Scatter plots can be used to identify relationships, trends, patterns, clusters, and outliers among the data points.

A common use case is to  plot an independent variable (e.g. time) on the x-axis and a dependent variable on the y-axis.

Scatter plots allow you to visually assess how strongly two variables are correlated.

Frequenty, scatter plots feature regression lines.

Like line graphs, the x and y axes of scatter plots are cropped. This is because the purpose of the plot is to show relationship, not magnitude.

hierarchy.lvl2: Createing a scatter plot from scratch
Createing a scatter plot from scratch

records.content:
To understand the design and purpose of a scatter plot, let’s build one from scratch.

We’ll create one out of some random numeric data.

We use NumPy’s random number generator that samples from the normal distribution to create a data frame with 1000 observations of 2 features.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns



df = pd.DataFrame({
    'f1': np.random.randn(1000),
    'f2': np.random.randn(1000)
})
df.head()



To understand the logic of a scatter plot, consider how we’d create one by hand.

# Create figure and axes objects
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Scale the axes
ax.set_xlim(left=df.f1.min(), right=df.f1.max())
ax.set_ylim(bottom=df.f2.min(), top=df.f2.max())

# Plot each point
for idx, row in df.iterrows():
    plt.plot(row.f1, row.f2, '.', c='tab:blue')



Pandas’ .plot.scatter() method does this for us.

df.plot.scatter(x='f1', y='f2')
plt.show()



Because both features are drawn from the normal distribution, they should exhibit no correlation.

Indeed, the result is a random blob of points that cluster around 0, the mean.

Let’s look at a better example, one involve real data.

We import the Palmer Penguins data set from Seaborn.

This dataset represents body-size measurements for 344 penguins of three species observed on three islands of the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.

penguins = sns.load_dataset('penguins').dropna()
penguins



Here is a scatter plot of two features.

penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm')
plt.show()



Note that the plot effectively zooms in one the data by cropping the axes.

If the axes are not cropped, you get like this:

penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm', xlim=(0, None), ylim=(0, None))
plt.show()

hierarchy.lvl2: Showing a grouping variable with color
Showing a grouping variable with color

records.content:
If you want to map the distribution of species onto the figure, you can associate color with the variable.

Note

The ability to pass a feature name to c is only available in Pandas 3.

penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm', c='species')
plt.show()



The result shows that the observations cluster in the space created by the features.

This indicates that the features may be predictive of species.

Caution

If you pass to c a feature of the type category — which seems like a reasonable thing to do — the result will be different from what you see above. The legend will change to a segmented color bar on the right. Additionally, it may be necessary to set the cmap parameter, since one of the colors Pandas chooses in this context is white, which makes the points invisible.

We might also choose to change the size of each data point in proportion to a numeric variable.

Here we invent a feature size_factor to display for demonstration purposes.

We chould have just used body_mass_g, but this results in very large circles.

penguins['size_factor'] = (penguins.body_mass_g - penguins.body_mass_g.min())/10



penguins.plot.scatter(
    x='bill_length_mm', 
    y='bill_depth_mm', 
    s='size_factor', 
    alpha=.25)
plt.show()

It’s actually pretty easy to show four variables in a scatter plot.

Here we use both color and size as channels on which to map a categorical and numeric feature respectively.

Here we bump up the size of the figure to make clearly visible all four variables.

penguins.plot.scatter(
    x='bill_length_mm', 
    y='bill_depth_mm', 
    c='species',
    s='size_factor', 
    alpha=.25,
    figsize=(12, 10)
)
plt.show()
